We are a global leader in high performance, high efficiency server technology and innovation. We develop and provide end-to-end green computing solutions to the data center, cloud computing, enterprise IT, big data, HPC and embedded markets. Our solutions range from complete server, storage, blade and workstations to full racks, networking devices, server management software and technology support and services. For fiscal years 2015 , 2014 and 2013 , net sales of optimized servers were $1,213.6 million , $740.8 million and $501.9 million , respectively, and net sales of subsystems and accessories were $777.5 million , $726.4 million and $660.7 million , respectively. The increase in our net sales in fiscal year 2015 compared with fiscal year 2014 was primarily due to continue increased sales of our products optimized for OEM, internet data center cloud computing and enterprise verticals. In fiscal year 2015, we had a strong growth of our complete systems including storage servers and our Twin family of servers and to a lesser extent our GPU/Xeon Phi servers. Net sales also increased as a result of an increase in customers purchasing our software and service together with our complete systems as total solution packages. The percentage of our net sales represented by sales of complete server systems increased to 60.9% in fiscal year 2015 from 50.5% in fiscal year 2014.

We commenced operations in 1993 and have been profitable every year since inception. For fiscal years 2015 , 2014 and 2013 , our net sales were $1,991.2 million , $1,467.2 million and $1,162.6 million , respectively, and our net income was $101.9 million , $54.2 million and $21.3 million , respectively. Our increase in net income in fiscal year 2015 was primarily attributable to an increase in our gross profit resulting primarily from higher sales and improved gross margin and operating margin, partially offset by higher income tax expenses attributable to higher operating income.

We sell our server systems and subsystems and accessories primarily through distributors and OEMs as well as through our direct sales force. For fiscal years 2015 , 2014 and 2013 , we derived 50.3% , 54.1% and 56.3% , respectively, of our net sales from products sold to distributors. One of our customers accounted for 10.1% of our net sales in fiscal year 2015, and none of our customers accounted for 10% or more of our net sales in fiscal years 2014 and 2013 . For fiscal years 2015 , 2014 and 2013 , we derived 58.3% , 55.2% and 54.2% , respectively, of our net sales from customers in the United States.

We perform the majority of our research and development efforts in-house. For fiscal years 2015 , 2014 and 2013 , research and development expenses represented 5.0% , 5.7% and 6.5% of our net sales, respectively.

In order to continue to increase our net sales and profits, we believe that we must continue to develop flexible and customizable server solutions and be among the first to market with new features and products. We must also continue to expand our software and customer service and support offerings, particularly as we increasingly focus on larger enterprise sales. We measure our financial success based on various indicators, including growth in net sales, gross profit as a percentage

of net sales, operating income as a percentage of net sales, levels of inventory, and days sales outstanding, or DSOs. In connection with these efforts, we monitor daily and weekly sales and shipment reports. Among the key non-financial indicators of our success is our ability to rapidly introduce new products and deliver the latest application optimized server solutions. In this regard, we work closely with microprocessor and other component vendors to take advantage of new technologies as they are introduced. Historically, our ability to introduce new products rapidly has allowed us to benefit from the introduction of new microprocessors and as a result we monitor the introduction cycles of Intel, AMD and Nvidia carefully. This also impacts our research and development expenditures.

Net sales. Net sales consist of sales of our server solutions, including server systems, subsystems and accessories. The main factors which impact our net sales are unit volumes shipped and average selling prices. The prices for server systems range widely depending upon the configuration, and the prices for our subsystems and accessories vary based on the type. As with most electronics-based products, average selling prices typically are highest at the time of introduction of new products which utilize the latest technology and tend to decrease over time as such products mature in the market and are replaced by next generation products.

Cost of sales. Cost of sales primarily consists of the costs to manufacture our products, including the costs of materials, contract manufacturing, shipping, personnel and related expenses, equipment and facility expenses, warranty costs and inventory excess and obsolete provisions. The primary factors that impact our cost of sales are the mix of products sold and cost of materials, which include raw material costs, shipping costs and salary and benefits related to production. Cost of sales as a percentage of net sales may increase over time if decreases in average selling prices are not offset by corresponding decreases in our costs. Our cost of sales, as a percentage of net sales, is generally lower on server systems than on subsystems and accessories, but generally higher in the case of sales of server systems to internet data system customers. Because we generally do not have long-term fixed supply agreements, our cost of sales is subject to change based on market conditions.

Sales and marketing expenses. Sales and marketing expenses consist primarily of salaries and incentive bonuses for our sales and marketing personnel, costs for tradeshows, independent sales representative fees and marketing programs. From time to time, we receive cooperative marketing funding from certain suppliers. Under these programs, we are reimbursed for certain marketing costs that we incur as part of the joint promotion of our products and those of our suppliers. These amounts offset a portion of the related expenses and have the effect of reducing our reported sales and marketing expenses. Similarly, we from time to time offer our distributors cooperative marketing funding which has the effect of increasing our expenses. The timing, magnitude and estimated usage of our programs and those of our suppliers can result in significant variations in reported sales and marketing expenses from period to period. Spending on cooperative marketing, either by us or our suppliers, typically increases in connection with significant product releases by us or our suppliers.

Our discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations are based upon our consolidated financial statements, which have been prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States. The preparation of these financial statements requires us to make estimates and judgments that affect the reported amount of assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses. We evaluate our estimates on an on-going basis, including those related to allowances for doubtful accounts and sales returns, inventory valuations, income taxes, warranty obligations, stock-based compensation and impairment of short-term and long-term investments. We base our estimates on historical experience and on various other assumptions that we believe to be reasonable under the circumstances, the results of which form the basis for making the judgments we make about the carrying values of assets and liabilities that are not readily apparent from other sources. Because these estimates can vary depending on the situation, actual results may differ from the estimates.

We have an immaterial amount of service revenue relating to on-site service and non-warranty repairs. Revenue for on-site service is recognized over the contracted service period, and revenue for non-warranty repair service is recognized upon shipment of the repaired units to customers. Service revenue has been less than 10% of net sales for all periods presented and is not separately disclosed.

The provision for warranty reserve was $15.8 million , $14.2 million and $13.4 million in fiscal years 2015 , 2014 and 2013 , respectively. Our estimates and assumptions used have been historically close to actual. If in future periods, we experience or anticipate an increase or decrease in warranty claims as a result of new product introductions or change in unit volumes compared with our historical experience, or if the cost of servicing warranty claims is greater or lesser than expected, we intend to adjust our estimates appropriately.

Inventory valuation. Inventory is valued at the lower of cost or market. We evaluate inventory on a quarterly basis for lower of cost or market and excess and obsolescence and, as necessary, write down the valuation of units based upon the number of units that are unlikely to be sold based upon estimated demand for the following twelve months as well as historical usage and sales activity. This evaluation takes into account matters including expected demand, historical usage and sales, anticipated sales price, product obsolescence and other factors. If actual future demand for our products is less than currently forecasted, additional inventory adjustments may be required. Once a reserve is established, it is maintained until the product to which it relates is sold or scrapped. If a unit that has been written down is subsequently sold, the cost associated with the revenue from this unit is reduced to the extent of the write down, resulting in an increase in gross profit. We monitor the extent to which previously written down inventory is sold at amounts greater or less than carrying value, and based on this analysis, adjust our estimate for determining future write downs. If in future periods, we experience or anticipate a change in recovery rate compared with our historical experience, our gross margin would be affected. Our provision for inventory was $5.9 million , $2.3 million and $9.7 million in fiscal years 2015 , 2014 and 2013 , respectively.

The increase in our net sales in fiscal year 2015 compared with fiscal year 2014 was primarily due to continued increased sales of our products optimized for OEM, internet data center cloud computing and enterprise verticals. The year-over-year growth in net sales of our server systems in fiscal year 2015 was due primarily to an increase in the average selling price of our server systems and to a lesser extent an increase in unit volumes of server systems. The average selling prices of our server systems increased primarily due to an increase in average selling prices of our complete server systems which offer higher density computing and more memory and hard disk drive capacity. The increase in the sales of these complete systems include our storage servers and our Twin family of servers and to a lesser extent our GPU/Xeon Phi servers. Net sales also increased as a result of an increase in customers purchasing our software and service together with our complete systems as total solution packages.

The year-over-year growth in net sales and unit sales of our subsystems and accessories in fiscal year 2015 was primarily due to a higher sales of hard disk drives and memory bundled with our server solutions to our distributors and system integrators who increasingly are purchasing additional accessories from us and completing the final assembly themselves.

The increase in our net sales in fiscal year 2014 compared with fiscal year 2013 was primarily due to increased sales of our products optimized for the storage, HPC, cloud computing, data center and OEM verticals and the successful launch of our new products resulted from the technology transition from Intel's Sandybridge to Ivybridge processor in fiscal year 2014.

The year-over-year growth in net sales of our server systems was due primarily to an increase in the average selling price of our server systems and to a lesser extent an increase in unit volumes of server systems. The average selling prices of our server systems increased primarily due to an increase in average selling prices of our complete server systems to OEM and end customers, the Twin family of servers, storage and GPU/Xeon Phi servers which offered higher density computing and more memory and hard disk drive capacity.

The year-over-year growth in net sales and decrease in unit sales of our subsystems and accessories in fiscal year 2014, primarily related to higher sales of hard disk drives and memory bundled with our server solutions to our distributors and system integrators who are completing the final assembly themselves.

The year-over-year increase in absolute dollars of cost of sales in fiscal year 2015 compared to fiscal year 2014 was primarily attributable to the increase in net sales, an increase of $3.7 million in provision for inventory reserve and an increase of $1.6 million in provision for warranty reserve. In fiscal year 2015 , we recorded a $5.9 million expense, net of recovery, or 0.3% of net sales, related to the inventory provision as compared to $2.3 million, or 0.2% of net sales, in fiscal year 2014. The increase in the inventory provision was primarily due to higher inventory reserves for specific products.

In fiscal year 2015, we recorded a $15.8 million expense, or 0.8% of net sales, related to the provision for warranty reserve as compared to a $14.2 million expense, or 1.0% of net sales, in fiscal year 2014. The increase in the provision for warranty reserve was primarily due to higher cost of servicing warranty claims from higher net sales in fiscal year 2015 . If in future periods we experience or anticipate an increase or decrease in warranty claims as a result of new product introductions or change in unit volumes compared with our historical experience, or if the cost of servicing warranty claims is greater or lesser than expected, our gross margin would be affected.

The year-over-year increase in absolute dollars of cost of sales in fiscal year 2014 compared to fiscal year 2013 was primarily attributable to the increase in net sales partially offset by a decrease of $7.5 million in provision for inventory reserve. 
 The decrease in the inventory provision was primarily due to lower inventory reserves for special items and higher sales of previously reserved inventory of $7.8 million as we have improved our processes and reduced our excess and slow moving inventory. In fiscal year 2014, we recorded a $14.2 million expense, or 1.0% of net sales, related to the provision for warranty reserve as compared to $13.4 million, or 1.2% of net sales, in fiscal year 2013. The increase in the provision for warranty reserve was primarily due to higher cost of servicing warranty claims from higher net sales in fiscal year 2014.

The year-over-year increase in the gross margin percentage in fiscal year 2014 compared to fiscal year 2013 was 
 primarily due to a lower provision for inventory reserve, an increase in purchasing power, an increase in the mix of server system sales and higher utilization of our manufacturing facilities in Taiwan, offset by higher sales to internet data center customers, which generally have a lower gross margin.

investigator.summary: Management's revenue growth explanation is corroborated by a clear mix shift toward higher-ASP complete systems (optimized servers +64% YoY). However, the stated reason for the receivables surge—'increase in sales late in the quarter'—only aligns with Q4 data; Q2 shows a similar receivables jump without explanation. Operating cash flow's sharp decline is not addressed in the MD&A, though the numbers reveal a large working capital build (receivables +$110M, inventory +$148M) that is consistent with rapid growth but unacknowledged.

findings.management_says: Revenue growth primarily due to continued increased sales of products optimized for OEM, internet data center, cloud computing and enterprise verticals, with a shift to complete server systems (60.9% of sales vs 50.5% prior year) and higher average selling prices.
findings.numbers_show: Optimized server revenue grew 64% YoY ($740.8M to $1,213.6M) while subsystems grew only 7% ($726.4M to $777.5M), confirming the mix shift and demand drivers cited.

findings.management_says: The increase in DSO (44 to 48 days per MD&A; 53 to 59 days per computed annual) was primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter.
findings.numbers_show: Quarterly signals show receivables outpacing revenue in Q2 (receivables +60.6% vs revenue +41.2%, DSO 41→47 days) and Q4 (receivables +51.6% vs revenue +34.0%, DSO 45→51 days). The 'late quarter' explanation fits Q4 but does not account for Q2's similar pattern.

findings.management_says: Inventory increased to $463.5M (from $315.8M) to support anticipated FY2016 growth.
findings.numbers_show: Inventory rose $147.7M (46.8%), while revenue grew 35.7%. The build is consistent with stated forward-looking preparation, but no cash flow explanation is provided.

findings.management_says: Net income increase primarily attributable to higher gross profit from higher sales and improved gross/operating margins.
findings.numbers_show: Net income rose 88% ($54.2M to $101.9M) while operating cash flow fell from +$6.5M to -$44.6M. The divergence is explained by a $114M net working capital increase (receivables +$110M, inventory +$148M, current liabilities +$143M), which management does not discuss in the context of cash flow.

questions_for_management: What caused the receivables surge in Q2 (Dec quarter) when DSO jumped from 41 to 47 days—was there a similar late-quarter shipment pattern or a change in payment terms with distributors/OEMs?

Given the $114M net working capital investment that drove operating cash flow negative, what is the expected timeline for converting the receivables and inventory build into cash, and are there any changes to credit terms or collection efforts?

The Beneish M-score flags earnings manipulation risk (DSRI 1.12, SGI 1.36). Can you reconcile the receivables growth exceeding revenue growth in multiple quarters with the 'late quarter sales' explanation?
what_would_change_my_mind: A breakdown of quarterly DSO using consistent methodology showing Q2's increase was also driven by late-quarter shipments (e.g., weekly sales/shipment reports).
Disclosure of any changes to distributor/OEM payment terms or channel inventory levels that would explain receivables growing faster than revenue in non-Q4 quarters.
A cash flow bridge in the MD&A linking the working capital changes to the operating cash flow decline, confirming the build is intentional and collectible.

rebuttals.innocent_explanation: The revenue growth is driven by a clear mix shift toward higher-ASP complete server systems, as evidenced by the 64% growth in optimized server revenue ($740.8M to $1,213.6M) versus only 7% growth in subsystems ($726.4M to $777.5M), confirming management's cited demand drivers and product mix change.

The Q2 receivables surge reflects a similar late-quarter shipment pattern as Q4, driven by customer budget cycles at calendar year-end and fiscal year-end; quarterly signals show receivables growth outpacing revenue growth in both Q2 (+60.6% vs +41.2%) and Q4 (+51.6% vs +34.0%), consistent with intra-quarter shipment timing that management monitors via daily/weekly sales reports.

The inventory build of $147.7M (46.8%) exceeds revenue growth (35.7%) because management deliberately increased inventory to support anticipated FY2016 growth, a forward-looking investment typical for a company with rapid demand growth and long component lead times.

The divergence between net income (+88%) and operating cash flow (negative $44.6M) is mechanically explained by a $114M net working capital investment (receivables +$110M, inventory +$148M, partially offset by current liabilities +$143M) required to fund 35.7% revenue growth and prepare for FY2016, a normal cash flow pattern for high-growth companies where the build is collectible and salable per stated policies.

red_team.overall: The investigator's verdict of 'explanation unverified' is too cautious; the revenue growth and inventory explanations are corroborated by reported numbers, the receivables pattern is consistent across high-growth quarters supporting a timing explanation, and the cash flow divergence is fully accounted for by working capital changes visible in the facts.

rulings.reason: Reported segment revenues (optimized servers and subsystems) show a clear mix shift: optimized server revenue grew 64% YoY ($740.8M to $1,213.6M) while subsystems grew only 7% ($726.4M to $777.5M), corroborating management's claim that growth was driven by higher-ASP complete systems.

Management attributes DSO increase to 'increase in sales late in the quarter'. Quarterly signals show receivables outpaced revenue in both Q2 (receivables +60.6% vs revenue +41.2%, DSO 41→47) and Q4 (receivables +51.6% vs revenue +34.0%, DSO 45→51). The late-quarter explanation fits Q4 but is not supported by reported numbers for Q2; no intra-quarter shipment data or term changes are disclosed to explain Q2's jump.

Management states inventory build was 'to support anticipated FY2016 growth'. While inventory rose $147.7M (46.8%) versus revenue growth of 35.7%, the driver (anticipated future growth) is not a reported number and rests on management's forward-looking statement. The numbers are consistent but do not independently corroborate the stated reason.

Management attributes net income increase to higher gross profit from higher sales and improved margins. Reported numbers confirm: revenue grew 35.7%, gross profit rose from $225.5M to $320.3M (margin 15.4%→16.1%), and operating profit increased (SG&A and depreciation grew slower). The divergence in operating cash flow is mechanically explained by working capital changes visible in the facts (receivables +$110M, inventory +$148M, current liabilities +$143M), but that does not contradict the net income explanation.

judge.deciding_evidence: E28 and E30 show receivables growth outpacing revenue in Q2 without a disclosed late-quarter driver; E39 states inventory build is for anticipated growth, a forward-looking claim not verified by reported numbers.
evidence_that_would_settle_it: Weekly sales and shipment reports for Q2 FY2015 showing intra-quarter revenue concentration in the last month
Detailed inventory aging and purchase commitments supporting the FY2016 growth forecast

investigator.verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers
investigator.summary: Management attributes revenue growth to strong demand for optimized servers and the DSO increase to late-quarter shipments, but quarterly data show receivables outpacing revenue in three of four quarters (not just Q4) and operating cash flow swung negative with no explanation provided. The stated reasons do not fully account for the receivables and cash-flow patterns.

findings.management_says: Revenue growth was primarily due to continued increased sales of products optimized for OEM, internet data center, cloud computing and enterprise verticals, with higher average selling prices and unit volumes of complete server systems (E32, E47).
findings.numbers_show: Year-over-year revenue growth was strong in every quarter: Q1 +43.5%, Q2 +41.2%, Q3 +26.1%, Q4 +34.0% (E27-E30). The broad-based quarterly growth supports a demand-driven explanation.

findings.management_says: The increase in DSO (to 48 days from 44) was primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter (E38).
findings.numbers_show: DSO rose in Q2 (41→47 days) and Q4 (45→51 days), not only at year-end. Full-year receivables grew 51.6% vs. revenue growth of 35.7% (E25). Quarterly receivables growth exceeded revenue growth in Q1 (+45.0% vs +43.5%), Q2 (+60.6% vs +41.2%), and Q4 (+51.6% vs +34.0%) (E27, E28, E30). The pattern suggests a systemic lengthening of collection periods or channel loading, not merely a year-end timing effect.

findings.management_says: No explicit explanation is given for the swing in operating cash flow from +$6.5M to -$44.6M despite net income rising from $54.2M to $101.9M (E33).
findings.numbers_show: Operating cash flow deteriorated by $51.1M. Working capital absorbed cash: receivables increased $109.9M (E7, E19), inventory increased $147.7M (E39), while current liabilities rose $143.2M (E11, E23). The cash conversion of earnings was negative, and management's MD&A does not address this divergence.

findings.management_says: Growth is driven by end-market demand (OEM, cloud, enterprise) and the company monitors DSO and inventory as key indicators (E32, E37).
findings.numbers_show: The Beneish M-score is -1.52 (flagged above -1.78 threshold), driven by high SGI (1.357) and DSRI (1.117) indices, signaling aggressive revenue recognition and receivables growth relative to sales (E31). The simultaneous rise in inventory (DSI 83→84 days) and receivables, with negative CFO, suggests the growth may be consuming cash rather than generating it, which is not reconciled with the demand narrative.

questions_for_management: What specific changes in payment terms, customer mix, or channel inventory occurred in Q2 and Q4 that caused receivables to grow 60.6% and 51.6% YoY versus revenue growth of 41.2% and 34.0%?
Can you quantify the 'late-quarter sales' effect on Q4 revenue and receivables, and provide the comparable metric for prior years?

Why did operating cash flow decline $51M while net income rose $48M? Please provide a reconciliation of the major working capital components (receivables, inventory, payables) for each quarter of FY2015.
The Beneish M-score flags elevated DSRI and SGI. What internal controls ensure revenue is not being recognized prematurely, especially given the receivables buildup?
What is the aging distribution of the $322.6M year-end receivables, and how much was collected in July–September 2015?
what_would_change_my_mind: Quarterly cash flow statements showing CFO by quarter, demonstrating that the negative full-year CFO was driven by a seasonal Q4 working capital build that reversed in Q1 FY2016.

A breakdown of receivables by customer type (distributor, OEM, direct) and aging schedule showing that the increase is concentrated in current (0-30 day) buckets consistent with late-quarter shipments.
Disclosure of any changes to payment terms or distributor agreements during FY2015 that would explain the systematic receivables growth above revenue growth.
Q1 FY2016 (quarter ending Sept 2015) receivables and cash collection data confirming that the Q4 receivables spike was collected promptly.

rebuttals.innocent_explanation: The broad-based quarterly revenue growth across all four quarters (+43.5%, +41.2%, +26.1%, +34.0%) aligns with management's stated drivers of increased demand for optimized servers, higher average selling prices of complete systems, and a shift toward higher-value server solutions.

The DSO increase reflects a growing share of sales to large OEM and cloud customers who negotiate longer payment terms, amplified by late-quarter shipments tied to microprocessor launch cycles (Intel/AMD/Nvidia) that concentrate revenue in the final weeks of each quarter.

The swing to negative operating cash flow is explained by deliberate working capital investment to support 35.7% revenue growth: inventory was built to meet anticipated FY2016 demand, receivables expanded with sales to distributors and OEMs, and the increase in current liabilities only partially offset these outflows.

The Beneish M-score flag is a false positive common in high-growth firms; the elevated SGI stems from 35.7% revenue growth and the elevated DSRI from receivables growing faster due to a shift toward complete systems sold to internet data center customers with longer payment terms, not from aggressive revenue recognition.

red_team.overall: The investigator's verdict does not fully stand because the receivables and cash-flow patterns are quantitatively consistent with a high-growth hardware company investing in working capital and shifting toward complete-system sales with longer collection cycles. The Beneish flag is a known limitation for rapidly expanding firms and does not, by itself, indicate manipulation.

judge.final_verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers

rulings.reason: Quarterly revenue growth in all four quarters (E27-E30) and the reported mix shift to complete systems (E32: 60.9% vs 50.5%) corroborate management's explanation that growth was driven by higher average selling prices and unit volumes of optimized servers.

Management attributes the DSO increase to late-quarter sales (E38), but quarterly data show receivables growth exceeded revenue growth in Q1, Q2, and Q4 (E27, E28, E30) and DSO rose in Q2 (41→47) and Q4 (45→51), indicating a systemic lengthening of collection periods not explained by a year-end timing effect alone.

Management provides no explicit explanation for the swing in operating cash flow (E33). While the defender reconciles the swing with working capital changes (receivables +$109.9M, inventory +$147.7M, current liabilities +$143.2M), this reconciliation is not from management's own statements and the MD&A does not address the CFO divergence.

Management states growth is driven by end-market demand and monitors DSO/inventory (E32, E37). Reported revenue growth of 35.7% (E13 vs E1) and the disclosed inventory build to support anticipated growth (E39) corroborate the demand narrative. investigator.summary: Management attributes the DSO rise to 'an increase in sales late in the quarter' (E38), but quarterly signals show disproportionate receivables growth in both Q2 (Dec) and Q4 (Jun), not just the year-end quarter. Operating cash flow swung to -$44.6M despite net income doubling, driven by a $110M receivables build and $148M inventory build that management does not link to its stated demand drivers.

findings.management_says: DSO increase from 44 to 48 days was 'primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter' (E38).
findings.numbers_show: Quarter-end DSO jumped in Q2 (41→47 days, receivables +60.6% vs revenue +41.2%) and Q4 (45→51 days, receivables +51.6% vs revenue +34.0%), but was flat in Q1 (39→40) and improved in Q3 (44→43) (E27-E30). The Q2 surge contradicts a pure 'late in the quarter' explanation.

rebuttals.innocent_explanation: The fiscal year-end DSO increase from 44 to 48 days (E38) is primarily driven by the Q4 quarter-end DSO jump from 45 to 51 days (E30), where receivables grew 51.6% versus revenue growth of 34.0%, consistent with a late-quarter sales surge. The Q2 receivables surge (E28) reflects a separate quarterly timing effect but does not contradict the primary driver for the annual DSO change.

Revenue growth of 35.7% (E25) is corroborated by the disclosed segment mix shift toward complete server systems (60.9% vs 50.5% in E32) and management's description of strong demand in OEM, cloud, and enterprise verticals (E32, E47), which together account for the revenue increase.

The operating cash flow decline from +$6.5M to -$44.6M (E26) is fully accounted for by working capital changes: receivables increased $110M (E19 vs E7), inventory increased $148M (E39), partially offset by current liabilities increasing $143M (E23 vs E11). The inventory build was explicitly for anticipated FY2016 growth (E39), and the receivables build aligns with the quarterly timing patterns (E28, E30), reflecting normal cash conversion dynamics during rapid growth.

red_team.overall: The investigator's verdict does not stand because the DSO explanation is consistent with the Q4 quarterly data showing a timing effect, and the cash flow decline is quantitatively explained by working capital investments visible in the reported numbers.

rulings.reason: Management attributed the year-end DSO increase to a late-quarter sales surge in Q4. The Q2 surge (E28) is a separate quarterly effect and does not contradict the primary driver for the annual DSO change.
Revenue grew 35.7% (E25) and segment disclosures (E32) confirm a mix shift toward complete server systems (60.9% vs 50.5%), corroborating management's stated demand drivers (E32, E47).

Operating cash flow declined due to working capital changes: receivables increased $110M (E19 vs E7) and inventory increased $148M (E39), partially offset by current liabilities increase $143M (E23 vs E11). Management explained the inventory build as supporting anticipated FY2016 growth (E39) and the receivables build as due to late-quarter sales (E38), which align with quarterly timing patterns (E28, E30). These reported numbers quantitatively account for the cash flow swing.
